claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is predominantly maintained by the combined effects of atomic-size mismatch and chemical disorder.
Atomic-size mismatches create local lattice strain.
Chemical disorder produces heterogeneous energy barriers that impede atomic diffusion.
A near-equimolar disordered AlCrCoFeNi-type nanoalloy has inherent atomic-size differences among its elements.
Artificially homogenizing effective atomic radii while retaining composition removes size-induced strain.
Temperatures of 1500–2200 K activate thermal diffusion and possible phase transitions in the proposed nanoalloy.
Atomic-size mismatch produces localized strain that elevates atomic-migration barriers.
The nonuniform energy landscape associated with chemical disorder hinders atom hopping.
Reduced atomic diffusion suppresses grain-boundary migration and phase separation.
The naturally size-mismatched nanoalloy will have a significantly lower atomic diffusion coefficient than the equal-radius control.
The naturally size-mismatched nanoalloy will form fewer chemical clusters than the equal-radius control.
The naturally size-mismatched nanoalloy will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure better than the equal-radius control.
Uniform atomic radii will promote atomic mobility, clustering, or phase demixing.
In AlxCrCoFeNi, the relatively large size of Al considerably changes lattice ordering and Al content changes the stable phase constitution.
The prediction is limited to high temperatures below complete melting.
The predicted effect applies to near-equimolar nanoalloys with atomic-size mismatch greater than approximately 5%.
Comparable diffusion and phase evolution in the natural and equal-radius models would falsify size-mismatch-induced strain as the dominant stability factor.
